## My Reasoning

My family has farmed this land in Quzhou my whole life. We have about 12 mu of flat, well-irrigated land here on the North China Plain. There's really no question about what I grow — winter wheat then summer maize, every year, same as my father and the neighbors. That rotation makes sense here. The land is suited to it, the markets are there for both, and I know how to do it.

Come October I plant wheat across all 12 mu. I've been using Jimai 22 for a few years now — got it from the township seed station, it holds up fine against rust and gives decent yields. I apply a solid base dressing of fertilizer before planting and then topdress at jointing. I don't scrimp on nitrogen. I've had years where I cut back and the yield showed it. So I put down about 18 kg of N per mu total — some upfront, some at the joint stage. Same goes for phosphorus in the base, less potassium.

Wheat needs water here — rain alone won't do it. I irrigate four times: winter irrigation to protect roots from frost heave, green-up water in late February, jointing water in April, and a grain-filling irrigation in May. That's just standard here. For pest management, I spray herbicide once in early spring for the weeds, one fungicide pass when I see signs of powdery mildew or rust moving through the county, and I spray for aphids near heading — so three applications total.

Right after wheat harvest in mid-June I turn around fast and plant maize on the same 12 mu. Always hybrid seed —郑单958 or whatever the station has that year. No-one around here uses traditional corn anymore. I do rotary tillage for the maize seedbed, quick and cheap between the two crops. Summer maize gets plenty of rain usually, so I only irrigate once or twice if July turns dry. Maize gets similar nitrogen — 18 kg/mu split across base and two side-dressings. Herbicide once after emergence, pest spray once for corn borer or armyworm if the extension office sends out a warning. Two applications is usually enough.

I expect about 450 kg of wheat per mu and 550 kg of maize per mu. Not the highest in the county, but reliable.
